I want every writer we hire to leave eventually.

If they don't, I've probably hired the wrong person.

Most companies treat ambition like a flight risk.

They screen for loyalty and act betrayed when someone good moves on.

I think that's backwards.

I left Goldman Sachs to go and sell burgers. I'm not going to hire people and then ask them to stop wanting the same thing.

At Draper we look for people who want to build something of their own one day.

People building towards something treat a client's problems like practice for their own.

They move faster.

They care more.

So while they're here, they get the real thing. They run the founder call themselves and get paid for every client they take on.

If someone learns everything here and leaves to start a company, that's the plan working.

You can train skill.

You can't teach hunger.

P.S. We're hiring content strategists who want to build something of their own one day. Full role in the comments.

Last October I fell asleep at the wheel in traffic and drove into the back of the car in front of me.

Nobody was hurt.

It took me a long time to stop thinking about the version where somebody was.

I was setting up Peruvian Street Kitchen at the time, still running the dark kitchen for Simply Smashed, and taking Draper meetings on top of both.

Which meant the only window Mustafa and I could find each other in was six, seven in the morning, before service.

So I'd take those, work the kitchen through the day, and then pick the rest back up late into the night.

Every day, because there was no other way to fit it.

I was a bit proud of the hours at the time. That was the tell.

Because the thing I'd built only worked as long as I personally never stopped. That isn't a company, that's just me being a bottleneck with a logo on it.

And you don't fix a bottleneck by grinding harder, which was the only move I actually knew.

So we hired. And we cut the week in half: every client call stacked into Monday and Wednesday, the other three days left completely alone for building.

It sounds like nothing. It's the reason there are now whole days where I'm not the thing everyone is waiting on.

It's still early and it's still intense. But Draper doesn't run on how much sleep I got anymore.

P.S the guy I went into was called Adam. We swapped details there in the traffic and he couldn't have been nicer about it.

We spent the first few months of Draper arguing about our moat.

Then the clients showed up and the argument stopped, because nobody had time for it:

The question was real. Would the models move under us. Were we a wrapper, the word that followed every AI company around that year.

We knew what people wanted. We could see it plain as day.

And instead of running at it, we kept stopping to ask whether they'd still want it in six months.

There was never a moment where we answered that.

Demand just started arriving faster than we could think about it, and suddenly the whole week was serving the people we had and building for the ones on their way.

Which is what we should have been doing from day one.

The moat question was a way of not doing the work. It felt like strategy. It was mostly fear with a whiteboard.

A GP I follow reckons moats are dead now.

His friend runs a company doing close to a billion in revenue and has taken one week off in eight years, because he sells AI to the smartest people alive and the second the product slips, they leave.

Sounds terrifying. Weirdly, it settled me.

Because that man's moat is the eight years. It's the showing up, and there is no version of it you can find before you've done the showing up.

Harvey got called a wrapper for a year. They lived long enough to train their own models, and nobody calls them that now.

We're a long way from a billion. But the question stopped mattering the week the calendar filled, and I think that's the only way it ever does.

One of my front of house guys at Simply Smashed found out about the Goldman bit mid-shift and just went "you left Goldman Sachs for this?"

He wasn't taking the piss either. He actually felt sorry for me.

Goldman Sachs, then a social media startup, then a burger shop, then a ghostwriting agency, now an AI content startup.

Everyone gets stuck on the burger bit and it's the least interesting jump on there.

Goldman put me on a team nobody had a plan for, which is how I ended up in a prayer room asking a guy about the janky donation app he'd coded himself, and then working on it.

There were four of us. I did users and support, worked out what we should build next, and posted about all of it on Twitter. One of those posts went viral during Ramadan and thousands of people ended up donating pennies through it.

Then Simply Smashed.

We set the dark kitchen up, then I left to study in Egypt for nine months while my brother and my dad kept it running.

I came back and my brother gave me one rule. Your job is to grow it.

And there were long stretches in there where I thought the front of house guy had a point.

When you're inside it every day you can't tell whether any of it is working, and I'd catch myself wondering if I should have stayed in tech.

We had nothing to spend so I used what I already knew worked, got into how the kitchen ran and what we were putting out, and told the story publicly the whole way through.

It ended up the highest rated burger joint in London.

Which got me in the door at the agency, where I trained the writers and worked out that the instinct I'd been running on since I was 19 was an entire industry. One that AI was about to turn over completely.

I didn't fancy watching that happen from inside someone else's company.

So, Draper.

I don't think I ever actually answered him.

I got 6 A*s and 5 As at GCSE.

Then I got BBDD at A-level.

Nobody's mentioned the GCSEs since. But I still hear about the A-levels.

At 16 I was coasting and I didn't even know it. I thought being smart was a personality trait and not something you actually had to maintain.

And A-levels are the moment the system stops rewarding you for being quick and starts asking if you can actually sit down and do the work.

I could not sit down and do the work.

BBDD hit and everyone knew. That's the thing about public failure when you've been publicly impressive, people do the maths for you.

But I think about it now and that was the first time I learned anything useful.

Everything I've built since, the restaurant, the agency career, Draper, came from a version of me that got humbled at 17 and finally figured out that showing up when it's boring is the entire game.

I live tweeted an entire demo day last month without typing a single word.

Last year I had ChatGPT open in a tab, a volunteer next to me snapping photos, and I was trying to live tweet Deen Developers demo day between pitches while half-listening to the next one. It was a mess but it kind of worked.

This year Draper just did it. Listened to every pitch, grabbed the photos as they came in, paired them with tweets and posted autonomously. I was sat there watching it happen and I'm not gonna lie I was gassed.

But the thing that actually got me is these founders have been building for weeks. And if nobody's covering it in real time, nobody outside the room ever knows.

Just some of the batch:

Amr → solo founder, one year old kid, built Lunchflow to £58k ARR and 20% monthly growth
Tarikh → Google Earth but for Islamic history
Stork → medical device compliance, £50k-£200k contracts six weeks in

All of that just gets missed if no one's there to put a spotlight on it. Draper picked that up on its own and I'm glad because otherwise it would've been another demo day where amazing people build amazing things and nobody gets to celebrate it.

The founders with the most interesting things to say are the ones who never have time to post.

Everyone knows volume matters. That's not controversial. Most founders fail at content because they're not posting enough and they know it. AI has made the volume problem basically solvable. You can generate a post about anything in seconds.

But volume without quality is just noise.

And quality is the bit that's actually hard to scale because it comes from somewhere specific. It comes from context. The thing you said on a call when you were explaining your vision to a new hire. A rant about why your industry does something backwards. The moment on a podcast where the cogs start turning and you forget anyone's listening.

That's what we've been building at Draper. We call it excavation. We plug into the places founders are already being brilliant and mine for the stuff that's actually worth posting. Their calls, their meetings, the moments where they go deep and the real thinking comes out.

AI collapses everything around that. The editing, the structuring, all the manual stuff that used to make content a full time job. (we're an AI content startup saying this btw, take from that what you will)

But as producing content gets easier, the thing that's actually going to be competitive is the angles. The excavation. The stuff that already lives in the best founders' heads. We just need to figure out how to get it out of you.

That's the problem we're trying to solve honestly. We're still cracking it but it's getting sharper every week.

What happens when you post a real Monet and say it's AI?

The coolest art social experiment I've seen in a while.

Someone posted a painting online and told people it was AI-generated. Asked them what made it inferior to the original.

"Looks like sh*t."
"Not as vibrant as Monet's typical palette."
"Achieving maybe 20% of the real thing."

People went in.

It was a real Monet. The actual painting.

And honestly the interesting thing here isn't the framing lesson everyone's pulling from this. It's what it tells you about where AI sentiment is right now.

People looked at a masterpiece and called it garbage because someone told them a machine made it. They weren't evaluating the painting at all. The word "AI" just did all the work before their eyes even caught up.

We run an AI native agency. The founders we work with are producing stuff that's good. Really good. But I know that if you slapped "AI-generated" on some of these posts, the same people who are engaging with them right now would suddenly call it slop. Same post, same words. You just changed what people think wrote it.

One of the founders we work with said something about this that stuck with me. If a human writes something mediocre, people think everyone has an off day. If AI writes something mediocre, people think zero effort.

That's the Monet experiment in one sentence.

I don't think the gap between what AI can actually do and what people think it can do is closing anytime soon.

We raised £26,000 for charity through an app where every like was worth 1p.

We made exactly £0 in revenue.

I was 18. First year of my degree apprenticeship at Goldman Sachs.

I met the co-founder in the basement prayer room. We'd just finished praying and I asked him how he was doing, just being polite, and he mistook it as me asking how the app was doing.

This man was probably mid-thirties, been at Goldman for years, and he just started telling me about this social media platform where every like triggered a micro-donation to charity.

I had no idea what he was talking about. But I was in.

That's how MiniDeed started for me. 1p, 2p, 5p. Tiny amounts that added up across 25 countries over two years. We onboarded Islamic Relief, Human Relief Foundation, a bunch of smaller orgs. We got featured in The New Arab. And somehow built a community where people were opening up about mental health because the whole vibe was just different. Users told us it was the only app where they felt safe doing that.

Honestly watching the live donation ticker go up was more addictive than any MRR dashboard I've looked at since (and I say that as someone who now stares at dashboards for a living).

We never figured out how to make money from it. Donations still trickle through the app daily, years later. But it was my first real taste of building something and I think about it all the time.

18 years old, sitting in Goldman Sachs by day, shipping a charity app by night. It led me to build the highest-rated burger joint in London. And now Draper.

Anthropic's been getting absolutely cooked last week. And then an OpenAI employee made it worse with two words.

Let me explain.

So Thariq, (Team Claude), announced they're tightening session limits during peak hours. People were already frustrated.

But then it gets worse.

People started suspecting Anthropic quietly dropped the baseline limits and ran a temporary 2x promo so the reduced limit feels normal. Promo ends, you're stuck at a lower baseline than before, and you don't even notice because the 2x absorbed the drop.

Sneaky if true and Anthropic denied the whole thing but the timeline is genuinely a mess.

And right in the middle of all this, Daniel Steigman, (Team Codex) just replies to the thread.

"thank you."

As in thank you for fumbling this so hard that your users are coming to us.

And the thing is it's not even a marketing play. OpenAI didn't run a campaign, they didn't post a comparison chart. One guy just typed "thank you" on a competitor's worst thread and walked away. That's just someone in the arena having fun and it ends up doing more for the brand than any campaign would.

This is what the AI race actually looks like now. It's not brand accounts posting press releases, it's employees with zero filter commenting like it's sports punditry. Researchers trash-talking each other and competitors lurking in each other's replies.

And the customers see ALL of it. Every interaction, every jab, every "thank you" is how brand perception actually forms now. Through the people, not the company page.
